topic: Forearm and wrist tension from mouse and keyboard

slides.headline: Your mouse hand deserves a break
slides.sub: Forearm and wrist tension from desk work, and what eases it.

slides.title: Small muscles, long hours
slides.body: Typing and mousing keep the forearm muscles gently working all day. They rarely get a proper break, so by Friday they can feel tight, achy or just plain tired.

slides.title: Check your desk setup
slides.body: Keep your elbows near your sides at about desk height and your wrists fairly flat. A mouse that fits your hand and a keyboard close to you cut down on reaching.

slides.title: Micro-breaks every half hour
slides.body: Drop your hands to your sides and shake them out, open and close your fists ten times, and gently stretch the wrists both ways. Thirty seconds is enough.

slides.title: Where remedial massage fits
slides.body: Massage through the forearms, upper arms and shoulders can ease tension and help your arms feel less heavy. It tends to work well combined with breaks and simple strength work.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Numbness or tingling in the fingers, pain waking you at night, weakness or dropping things, or swelling are worth assessing with a physio or GP rather than massaging.

slides.headline: Give your forearms a break
slides.body: Our remedial massage therapists work through the forearms, shoulders and neck, then suggest simple desk habits to keep things easing. Book online — link in bio.

caption:
Forearms feeling tight and heavy by the end of the week? Your mouse hand has been busy.

Typing and mousing keep small forearm muscles working for hours with barely a break. A few tweaks help: elbows by your sides at desk height, wrists fairly flat, and a mouse that actually fits your hand.

Every half hour, shake your hands out, open and close your fists and gently stretch your wrists. Remedial massage can ease the built-up tension, especially alongside these breaks. Numbness, tingling or weakness in the hand are worth getting assessed.
